title: Establish the physical mechanisms that store and retrieve a long-term memory

concept.text: The innovation would be a causal explanation of how a defined learned experience leaves physical changes in the brain, how those changes maintain information over time, and how later neural activity uses them to retrieve the memory. It would connect molecular processes, synaptic organization, distributed neural ensembles and observable behavior. Identifying neurons activated during learning or finding structural differences after learning supplies important evidence, but a complete account must explain what those changes do.

The target is a mechanism that can accommodate changing biological structures and neural participation. The supplied review describes partial overlap between ensembles involved in learning and recall, broader circuit involvement, and unresolved changes in synaptic architecture over time. A successful explanation would establish which features preserve the learned information, which enable access to it, and which are accompanying consequences of learning.

significance.text: A reproducible causal account would move beyond associating a memory with particular cells or synapses to explaining how an identified memory is maintained and retrieved. It would make the account experimentally predictive: selective changes to the proposed mechanism should produce specific, anticipated effects on retention or retrieval. This would connect physical organization to a lasting learned behavior across several levels of neuroscience.

Explaining memory maintenance despite biological turnover would be an additional achievement. Persistent morphology and a causal effect on retrieval would not, by themselves, show how information survives replacement or remodeling of its physical components. That stronger explanation would require tracking the relevant turnover and demonstrating the processes that preserve information through it. The supplied study does not establish such a mechanism.

Conditional synthesis: understanding these mechanisms could eventually inform treatments for memory impairment or interventions that modify particular memories. Human treatments and deliberate memory editing would require further advances and independent testing. A successful account of one animal memory would not automatically explain every memory type, human autobiographical experience or storage over decades. No historical comparison was supplied that would justify a stronger analogy.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central missing capability is to distinguish physical changes that carry and maintain learned information from changes that merely accompany learning or support general circuit function. The supplied manuscript identifies unresolved temporal dynamics, molecular composition and functional roles within the observed architecture. Resolving these questions requires connecting structural observations to selective causal tests and later behavior.

A major temporal barrier is determining when relevant changes form, how long they persist, and whether continued reorganization contributes to maintenance. The manuscript leaves open whether synaptic networks reorganize during a narrow period after learning or over a longer interval. Its seven-day structural snapshot cannot resolve those trajectories. Broader circuit involvement also means that observations within a hippocampal pathway cannot alone explain how a memory is maintained as systems consolidation proceeds.

Engineering synthesis: the needed experiments must link measurements across molecular, synaptic, circuit and behavioral scales while preserving the ability to interpret interventions. They must distinguish loss of stored information from impaired retrieval and exclude effects on perception, motivation or general circuit operation. If the explanation claims preservation through biological turnover, it must additionally measure replacement or remodeling and identify how the information survives those changes.

current_state.text: Uytiepo, Zhu et al., “Synaptic architecture of a memory engram in the mouse hippocampus,” was published in Science on March 21, 2025, DOI: 10.1126/science.ado8316. According to the supplied review of the full author manuscript, the study compared behaviorally tagged excitatory mouse hippocampal CA3–CA1 circuits. Optical imaging, electrophysiological and three-dimensional electron-microscopy analyses were conducted seven days after conditioning, before systems consolidation.

The study reported learning-associated synaptic and organelle differences, including reorganization involving multisynaptic boutons, or MSBs, in the CA1 stratum radiatum. The reported changes did not occur with exposure to a neutral conditioned stimulus, supporting a relationship between the learning condition and the observed architecture. The absence of preferential wiring between the compared activated neuronal populations also motivated the authors’ interpretation that those neurons participate in broader circuits. These findings do not establish which structural changes encode particular information or causally maintain it.

Retrieval behavior was assessed in separate cohorts; the animals used for circuit reconstruction did not undergo the retrieval protocol. Consequently, the reconstructed architecture was not directly tied to a retrieval test in those same animals. The manuscript also leaves unresolved the temporal dynamics of the observed changes and the molecular composition and functional role of MSBs. It advances the structural study of memory without supplying a complete causal explanation of storage and retrieval or evidence of decades-long persistence.

Evidence coverage is limited to the supplied review of a full, untruncated author-manuscript extraction. Linked supplements, figure images, movies and numerical data were not independently inspected in that review; prior manipulation studies discussed in the manuscript were not separately supplied. These limits constrain independent assessment of experimental detail without establishing that the reported findings are false. The supplied search record is empty, so this dated result does not establish the field’s status as of November 1, 2026, or whether subsequent work resolved any of these gaps.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: choose a defined, long-lasting memory in an animal preparation and specify the duration and behavior being explained. Identify the relevant physical changes across the necessary molecular, synaptic and circuit levels, track their persistence or transformation, and connect them to retention and later retrieval. Exhaustive atomic resolution of every component would not be required if the measurements resolve the mechanisms needed for the stated scope.
completion_criteria.label: Identified multilevel physical changes explain memory retention and later retrieval

completion_criteria.text: Proposed causal tests: use the mechanistic account to predict, before intervention, how selectively altering identified components will affect retention and retrieval. Test those predictions with controls that distinguish memory-specific effects from changes in perception, motivation or general circuit function. Where feasible, restoration or rescue experiments could help distinguish disruption of access from loss of the stored information. Independently reproduce the central causal results.
completion_criteria.label: Selective interventions confirm memory-specific causal predictions with independent reproduction

completion_criteria.text: Proposed extension: any claim to explain information preservation through biological turnover should include direct measurements of relevant replacement or remodeling and causal tests of the proposed preservation mechanism. Longer intervals and additional memory tasks would establish demonstrated breadth. These are proposed criteria, not established standards; finite experiments cannot establish literal universality, and a bounded animal result would not by itself establish a mechanism for human memories lasting decades.
completion_criteria.label: Measured biological turnover and causal tests establish information preservation mechanisms

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: BIO-09, “Observe and causally test whole-brain computation at cellular resolution,” overlaps through the need to measure and manipulate distributed neural activity. BIO-13 focuses specifically on the physical maintenance and retrieval of learned information across time. Whole-brain access could aid that investigation, but activity measurements alone would not establish molecular or synaptic storage mechanisms.

Roster-based synthesis: BIO-10, “Observe molecular state and dynamics inside living cells at scale,” could provide measurements of molecular persistence, renewal and remodeling relevant to memory. BIO-14, “Establish causal functions for noncoding elements and poorly understood proteins,” could help identify functions of molecular components implicated in maintenance. Both offer potentially enabling capabilities; neither alone connects those components to a specific learned experience and its later retrieval.

Roster-based synthesis: BIO-04, “Create an experimentally predictive virtual cell,” shares the goal of predictive biological mechanisms, but its cellular scope differs from the distributed circuit and behavioral explanation required here. BIO-15, “Deliver programmable genome editors selectively to diverse cells in the body,” could eventually enable selective perturbations of candidate mechanisms. Delivery capability would remain distinct from identifying which changes store information.

Roster-based synthesis: BIO-07, “Reversibly restore youthful function across an aged organism,” could intersect with memory preservation or recovery during aging. Restoring performance would not by itself explain the physical mechanisms of an identified memory, while explaining one memory would not establish organism-wide rejuvenation. More directly, BIO-13 connects to connectomics, synaptic plasticity and systems consolidation: circuit maps, learning-associated change and redistribution of memory dependence provide complementary parts of the mechanistic problem.

change_log.change: Preserved BIO-13 and its title while expanding the explanation across molecular, synaptic, circuit and behavioral levels.
change_log.reason: The research and review describe a multilevel mechanistic goal that should not be reduced to locating a structural correlate.

change_log.change: Specified the 2025 study’s seven-day interval, excitatory CA3–CA1 scope, structural findings and separate retrieval cohorts.
change_log.reason: These details establish what was examined and prevent interpreting the result as a direct causal demonstration of long-term storage and retrieval.

change_log.change: Made the explanation of memory preservation through biological turnover explicitly conditional and added corresponding proposed tests.
change_log.reason: Persistent structure and retrieval effects alone do not demonstrate information preservation during component replacement or remodeling.

change_log.change: Integrated unresolved temporal dynamics, MSB molecular composition and function, broader circuit involvement and systems consolidation into the scientific barriers.
change_log.reason: These distinctions explain why the reported architecture remains short of a complete mechanism.

change_log.change: Retained bounded animal demonstrations, prospective predictions, independent replication, behavioral controls and the absence of an atomic-resolution requirement as proposed completion criteria.
change_log.reason: They provide a concrete route to convincing evidence without presenting an editorial proposal as an established standard.

change_log.change: Separated the dated published result from present-day field status and preserved review coverage limitations.
change_log.reason: The supplied material contains no freshness search and does not independently assess supplements, images, movies, numerical data or underlying cited studies.

change_log.change: Added explicitly labeled roster-based relationships and conditional downstream implications.
change_log.reason: These explain overlap and practical significance without merging concepts or implying demonstrated human applications.

unresolved_issues: The supplied inputs do not establish whether later work resolved any of these gaps by November 2026.
The causal roles, molecular composition and temporal development of the reported MSB-associated changes remain unresolved in the supplied account.
The supplied study does not establish how memory information survives biological turnover or decades of storage.
Independent assessment of linked supplements, figures, movies, numerical data and prior studies would require evidence beyond the supplied review.
The proposed demonstration has no specified retention duration, memory task or intervention precision; these boundaries must be chosen for a concrete experimental program.

brief.title: An explanation of how lasting memories work
possible: We could explain how a particular experience leaves physical changes in the brain, how those changes keep a memory alive, and how the brain later uses them to remember. The explanation would link molecules, connections between nerve cells, and remembered behavior.

Researchers could predict how changing a particular part of that physical system would affect a specific memory. They could also distinguish a memory that has been lost from one that remains stored but cannot be reached.
why: For scientists studying memory, this would turn observations of brain changes into an explanation they could test. It would connect what happens inside cells with the lasting effects of learning.
Understanding how memories persist could eventually help researchers develop treatments for memory impairment or ways to modify particular memories.

sources.who: Marco Uytiepo, Yongchuan Zhu and colleagues
sources.showed: The team mapped connections between nerve cells in mice after learning. They found changes in connection size and organization, including more branching connections to other cells.
sources.quote: Neurons with a remote history of activity coinciding with memory acquisition showed no strong preference for wiring with each other.
sources.cited_for: Learning leaves physical changes in connections between nerve cells.
sources.not_established: The study did not establish which changes store information or cause later recall.

sources.showed: Disrupting the interaction between proteins called KIBRA and PKMζ impaired established memory for places without measurably affecting basic signaling between nerve cells.
sources.quote: KIBRA-PKMζ complexes maintain 1-month-old memory despite PKMζ turnover.
sources.cited_for: An ongoing interaction between proteins helps maintain memory despite replacement of a participating protein.
sources.not_established: This does not explain how a particular experience is represented across molecules, cell connections and brain circuits.

sources.showed: Weakening selected connections between nerve cells impaired recall of a particular event while sparing recall of another event in mice.
sources.cited_for: Specific connections can help distinguish memories that share participating nerve cells.
sources.not_established: Selective disruption of recall does not establish the full mechanism that stores and maintains a memory.

sources.who: Dheeraj S. Roy, Shruti Muralidhar, Lillian M. Smith and Susumu Tonegawa
sources.showed: In mice with drug-induced memory loss, activating learning-related cells with light produced recall when ordinary cues failed. Disrupting connections to downstream cells prevented this recall.
sources.quote: Here, we show that the full-fledged optogenetic recall persists at least 8 d after learning under protein synthesis inhibition-induced amnesia.
sources.cited_for: Failure to recall a memory through ordinary cues can differ from loss of the stored information.
sources.not_established: Artificial recall under drug-induced memory loss does not explain how ordinary long-term storage and retrieval work.

sources.who: Douglas Feitosa Tomé, Ying Zhang and colleagues
sources.showed: Computer models and mouse experiments showed that the groups of nerve cells involved in a memory change as it settles. Changes in connections that suppress activity helped memories become selective.
sources.quote: Our results reveal that memory engrams are dynamic and that changes in engram composition mediated by inhibitory plasticity are crucial for the emergence of memory selectivity.
sources.cited_for: An explanation of memory must accommodate changing participation by nerve cells.
sources.not_established: The results do not explain how learned information persists through long-term replacement of its physical components.

shown: Researchers have linked memory to physical structure, protein interactions and changing groups of nerve cells. Tsokas and colleagues found that a protein partnership maintained month-old memory despite replacement of one partner.

Roy and colleagues showed that mice could retain a memory they could not recall through ordinary cues. These findings establish parts of the explanation, but they do not yet connect a defined experience to a complete mechanism of lasting storage and later recall.
missing: A connected explanation must identify which physical changes carry a particular memory and which merely accompany learning.
Measurements must follow those changes over time and connect them to later recall in the same animals.
Selective tests must distinguish lost information from blocked access, while ruling out effects on perception, motivation or general brain function.

milestones.label: Physical changes explain lasting memory and later recall
milestones.explanation: A study would have to track the relevant molecules, cell connections and brain circuits for a defined animal memory over a stated interval. This would connect physical changes to remembering.

milestones.label: Selective changes confirm predictions, with independent reproduction
milestones.explanation: Selective interventions would have to produce predicted effects on a particular memory, with controls and independent reproduction. This would establish that the proposed mechanism causes storage and recall.

milestones.label: Memory survives measured replacement of its physical components
milestones.explanation: Measurements and causal tests would have to explain how information survives replacement or remodeling of the relevant components. This would explain persistence through biological change.

uncertain: The memory task, retention interval and precision of interventions needed for a convincing demonstration remain to be defined.
The roles and development over time of the branching connections observed after learning remain unresolved.
How far a mechanism established for a bounded animal memory would extend to human memories lasting decades remains open.

page.title: Mechanisms of long-term memory storage and retrieval
page.definition: A causal account explains how a defined learned experience is encoded, maintained and recalled through an engram—the lasting physical or chemical changes that store a memory. It explains how the information persists as relevant molecular components are replaced.

goal.need: In cultured rat cortical neurons, 191 synaptic proteins had a median estimated half-life of 3.67 days. In mice, disrupting KIBRA–PKMζ protein interactions impaired spatial memory tested 30 days after conditioning, with 9 treated and 7 control animals. Explaining memory therefore requires connecting molecular replacement to information retention, while distinguishing impaired retrieval from loss of stored information.

statements.quote: What neuronal, synaptic, biochemical and circuit mechanisms support working memory and long-term memory? How are memories retrieved?
statements.context: Questions identified in BRAIN 2025: A Scientific Vision.

statements.body: National Institute of Mental Health, Learning and Memory Program
statements.quote: What biological, systems-level mechanisms underlie how information is learned, recalled, and modified when needed?
To honor and highlight research into how learning and memory are physically encoded in the brain.
statements.context: The stated purpose of its annual research awards.

completion.title: One defined long-term memory has a causal explanation of its storage, maintenance and retrieval.
completion.criterion: For one specified species, learning task and retention interval, connect learning-induced physical changes to later cue-driven recall. Demonstrate observational, loss-of-function, gain-of-function, synaptic mimicry and transient-intervention erasure results within that memory preparation. Identify and experimentally test the process that preserves information through measured replacement of the proposed storage components. This is an Atlas synthesis of published criteria; it has no externally established universal duration or effect-size cutoff.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback, combining published engram-identification, synaptic mimicry and molecular-storage criteria.
completion.basis: Searches of NIH BRAIN and NIMH programmes, the Memory Decoding Challenge, engram-identification criteria, synaptic-plasticity criteria and molecular-erasure criteria found no integrated completion test. The decoding prize addresses reading information from connectivity. The narrow fallback concerns one experimentally bounded memory and combines causal identification with an explanation of persistence through turnover.

milestones.title: Learning leaves lasting cellular or synaptic changes in cells reactivated during memory retrieval.
milestones.criterion: Show overlapping cell populations during learning and retrieval, together with lasting learning-induced cellular or synaptic modifications. Structural evidence: published on 21 March 2025, Uytiepo et al. reconstructed mouse hippocampal circuitry after learning and found changes involving boutons that contact multiple postsynaptic structures. The bouton comparison included 3 fear-conditioned and 2 neutral-stimulus mice. Structural association alone does not satisfy the complete observational criterion.
milestones.set_by: Engram research convention articulated by Josselyn and Tonegawa in Science (2020), Experimental strategies to evaluate engrams; written for rodent studies.

milestones.title: Disrupting a memory's implicated cells or connections impairs subsequent retrieval.
milestones.criterion: After learning, impair the implicated cells or their connections and demonstrate impaired retrieval. Roy et al. blocked dentate-gyrus engram output to hippocampal CA3 and prevented light-induced recall, with 12 mice per group. Network-level evidence from Feitosa Tomé et al., published on 19 January 2024, showed that inhibiting CCK-positive interneurons during recall prevented context discrimination at 12 and 24 hours, with 9 inhibited and 7 control mice per delay. The latter identifies a contribution to selective retrieval.
milestones.set_by: Engram research convention articulated by Josselyn and Tonegawa in Science (2020), loss-of-function criterion; written for rodent studies.
milestones.threshold_quote: impairing engram cell function after an experience impairs subsequent memory retrieval.

milestones.title: Artificially activating learning-associated cells elicits recall without natural retrieval cues.
milestones.criterion: Activate the implicated cells artificially and elicit memory retrieval without the natural sensory retrieval cues. Published on 23 October 2017, Roy et al. reported light-induced contextual-fear recall 8 days after learning despite anisomycin-induced failure of natural recall. The 8-day comparison included 8 anisomycin-treated and 9 saline-treated mice. This demonstrates access to retained information under those conditions; it does not identify the molecular storage mechanism.
milestones.set_by: Engram research convention articulated by Josselyn and Tonegawa in Science (2020), gain-of-function criterion; written for rodent studies.
milestones.threshold_quote: artificially activating engram cells induces memory retrieval

milestones.title: Artificially imposing synaptic changes produces the predicted memory-guided behavior.
milestones.criterion: Artificially impose a distributed pattern of synaptic-strength changes and obtain the predicted behavior for an experience that did not occur or had been demonstrably forgotten. The published formulation requires manipulation at synapses rather than merely activating neuronal ensembles. Abdou et al., published on 15 June 2018, reported memory-specific potentiation and depotentiation in mouse auditory-fear circuits; the gain-of-function experiment used 10 mice per group. Reinstatement bears on the forgotten-memory version of this criterion.
milestones.set_by: Synaptic-plasticity research convention reviewed by Takeuchi, Duszkiewicz and Morris, section 3(d), Mimicry.
milestones.threshold_quote: a predictable display of ‘memory’ for something that in practice had either not happened or had happened earlier and then had been demonstrably forgotten.

milestones.title: Transient disruption leaves memory impaired after the intervention ends, while relearning remains possible.
milestones.criterion: Disrupt a proposed storage molecule after learning; test after the intervention has ended. The memory deficit persists, while relearning remains possible, addressing persistent damage as an alternative explanation. Published on 27 September 2017, Rossetti et al. reported impaired rat place avoidance 9 days after viral injection, following transient expression of mutant CaMKII, with 6 rats per group and subsequent relearning. A published commentary questioned the intervention's molecular specificity; the storage interpretation remains disputed.
milestones.set_by: Lisman's published Erasure test in Molecular Brain (2017), subsequently discussed and applied in the molecular-memory literature.
milestones.threshold_quote: it is crucial that the agent used to attack the putative memory molecule be applied and then removed before further testing.

not_found: No universal retention interval or effect-size cutoff was found in the reviewed engram criteria.
The supplied Uytiepo manuscript was blocked; its PubMed abstract and figure legends were accessible.

results.finding: In mice, learning-associated axons had about 1.6 times as many multi-synaptic boutons; 3 fear-conditioned and 2 neutral-stimulus mice were compared.
results.detail: Structural differences were assessed one week after conditioning. The reconstructed animals were not subjected to retrieval, so overlap between learning- and retrieval-active cells was not established.
results.quote: MSBs were present on both the (–) and (+) SchC axons of fear-conditioned mice, but their counts were ~1.6-fold higher on (+) axons.

results.finding: Two KIBRA-PKMζ antagonists disrupted long-term spatial memory; sample size not stated.
results.detail: The text does not report whether the memory impairment persisted after the intervention ended or whether relearning remained possible.
results.quote: Two structurally distinct antagonists of KIBRA-PKMζ dimerization disrupt established late-LTP and long-term spatial memory, yet neither measurably affects basal synaptic transmission.

results.finding: In mice, post-learning synaptic plasticity differed from nonshock controls; sample size not stated.
results.detail: The study reports synaptic changes and functional connectivity in learning-associated circuits, but the supplied text does not demonstrate overlap between cells active during learning and natural retrieval.

results.finding: Mouse CA3 and BLA learning-associated cells overlapped with recall-reactivated cells 8 days after training; n=3 per group.
results.detail: The study also measured spine density in labeled engram cells, but did not establish learning-induced lasting synaptic changes in the same reactivated cells.

results.finding: Blocking mouse DG engram output prevented light-induced fear recall; n=12 per group.
results.detail: The effect concerned optogenetic recall. Saline-treated mice with DG output blocked retained normal natural recall.
results.quote: These experiments demonstrate that an inactivation of engram cell connectivity downstream, but not upstream, prevents light-induced memory recall.

results.finding: Light activation elicited mouse fear recall 8 days after learning; n=8 anisomycin-treated and 9 saline-treated mice.
results.detail: Anisomycin-treated mice showed impaired natural recall. Artificial activation occurred in a distinct context.
results.quote: Here, we show that the full-fledged optogenetic recall persists at least 8 d after learning under protein synthesis inhibition-induced amnesia.

results.finding: PAK1 overexpression restored natural fear recall in amnesic mice 5 days after training; n=15 per group.

results.finding: In 11 mice, prefrontal engram connections were stronger 28 days after fear conditioning; learning-active neurons were also reactivated during recall.
results.detail: Recall reactivation and synaptic strengthening were assessed in related experiments; recordings compared learning-labeled engram neurons with nonengram neurons.
results.quote: Here we demonstrate that the consolidation of remote contextual fear memories in mice correlated with progressive strengthening of excitatory connections between prefrontal cortical (PFC) engram neurons active during learning and reactivated during remote memory recall, whereas the extinction of remote memories weakened those synapses.

results.detail: Four weeks after fear conditioning, freezing rose from 17.4% with the laser off to 29.6% with it on. The 9-mouse control group showed no corresponding increase.

results.detail: ZIP was given after memory reactivation, and a separate experiment reported relearning. The text does not establish that ZIP's intervention had ended before the memory test; its molecular specificity is also disputed.
